title: Health Assessment: General Survey, Vital Signs & Pain
html:
Health assessment turns observation, measurement, and the client's story into usable nursing information. The goal is not merely to collect numbers. The RN establishes a baseline, notices meaningful change, validates unexpected findings, identifies urgent threats, and communicates what the client needs next.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish subjective information from objective findings.
  • Begin with a general survey and a rapid safety scan.
  • Measure and interpret vital signs in context.
  • Complete a structured pain assessment and evaluate the response to care.
  • Recognize when an abnormal trend requires immediate action or escalation.

Start with the person

Introduce yourself, verify identity, explain the assessment, provide privacy, perform hand hygiene, and confirm that the environment is safe. Observe before touching equipment. The general survey includes apparent distress, level of consciousness, speech, work of breathing, skin appearance, posture, mobility, hygiene, and interaction. A rapid airway, breathing, circulation, and neurologic safety scan takes priority when instability is possible.

Assessment principle
Look at the client before deciding what a monitor value means. If the client appears unstable, call for help and begin focused assessment and immediate care; do not delay solely to repeat a measurement.

Subjective and objective data

Subjective data are experiences reported by the client, such as dizziness, nausea, fatigue, or pain quality. Objective data are observable or measurable findings, such as respiratory rate, skin temperature, behavior, blood pressure, or drainage. Validate unclear information, compare it with the record and baseline, and note the source when someone other than the client provides the history.

Vital signs are connected

Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and pain provide a snapshot of physiologic function. Interpret them together with age, diagnosis, medications, activity, position, oxygen delivery, recent procedures, symptoms, and prior values. A trend or an acute change from baseline may be more important than a single value that falls inside a reference range.

  • Temperature: record the value and route because measurement sites and devices are not interchangeable.
  • Pulse: assess rate, rhythm, strength, location, and symmetry when relevant. Count for a full minute when the rhythm is irregular or policy requires it.
  • Respirations: observe rate, rhythm, depth, effort, breath sounds when indicated, ability to speak, and oxygen use. Do not reduce breathing assessment to a monitor number.
  • Blood pressure: use a validated device and correctly sized cuff on bare skin; position and support the limb as required for the clinical situation. A cuff that is too small can produce an inaccurately high reading.
  • Oxygen saturation: assess the waveform or signal quality and the client. Motion, poor circulation, cold skin, nail products, device factors, and skin pigmentation can affect accuracy. Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation and must be interpreted with symptoms and other findings.

Validate without losing urgency

When a reading is unexpected, quickly check the client, technique, equipment, and comparison data. Repeat or confirm the measurement when appropriate. At the same time, watch for high-risk cues such as new altered mental status, severe work of breathing, inability to speak normally, cyanosis, weak perfusion, new chest pressure, rapidly changing vital signs, or a combination of abnormalities. Escalate according to the client's condition and the facility's response process.

Pain is multidimensional

The client's self-report is the primary source when the client can communicate. Use a consistent scale and explore PQRSTU: provoking or relieving factors, quality, region or radiation, severity, timing, and the client's understanding or impact on function. Also assess associated symptoms, prior effective strategies, goals, safety risks, and nonverbal behavior. A quiet appearance does not prove the absence of pain.

After an intervention, reassess at an appropriate time for the route and intervention. Compare pain intensity and function with the goal, check for adverse effects, and continue, modify, or escalate the plan. Giving an intervention without reassessment leaves the nursing process incomplete.

Focused versus comprehensive assessment

A comprehensive head-to-toe assessment establishes broad baseline information. A focused assessment answers a specific clinical question while still checking for immediate threats. For new shortness of breath, for example, the RN assesses appearance, airway, respiratory pattern and effort, oxygen delivery, lung sounds, circulation, mental status, relevant history, and trends—then acts and reassesses.

Document and communicate the change

Record the time, conditions of measurement, objective findings, the client's words, relevant comparison data, nursing actions, notifications, and response. Avoid vague conclusions such as “doing poorly.” When escalating, communicate the urgent concern first, followed by concise background, current assessment, actions already taken, and the response or request.

Clinical example

A postoperative client who was alert now answers slowly. The oxygen saturation display is lower than before, but the RN does not troubleshoot the device in isolation. The RN immediately assesses responsiveness, airway, breathing, circulation, oxygen delivery, and other vital signs; calls for appropriate help; checks the signal and probe; implements indicated care; and reassesses the response. The monitor provides a cue—the client determines the priority.
